'''''Malva arborea''''' (previously known as ''Lavatera arborea'', or, more recently as ''Malva eriocalyx''), the '''tree mallow''', is a species of mallow native to the [[coast]]s of western [[Europe]] and the [[Mediterranean region]], from [[Ireland]] and [[United Kingdom|Britain]] south to [[Algeria]] and [[Libya]], and east to [[Greece]].<ref name=mp>Malvaceae Pages: [http://www.malvaceae.info/Genera/Lavatera/arborea.html ''Lavatera arborea'']</ref><ref name=fe>Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Lavatera&SPECIES_XREF=arborea&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Lavatera arborea'']</ref><ref name=Botanica>''Botanica. The Illustrated AZ of over 10000 garden plants and how to cultivate them'' p. 514. Könemann, 2004. {{ISBN|3-8331-1253-0}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Lavatera arborea2.jpg|thumb|Flower]]
It is a [[shrub]]by [[annual plant|annual]], [[biennial plant|biennial]] or [[perennial plant]] growing to 0.5–2 m (rarely 3 m) tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are orbicular, 8–18 cm diameter, palmately lobed with five to nine lobes, and a coarsely serrated margin. The [[flower]]s are 3–4 cm diameter, dark pink to purple and grow in fasciculate axillary clusters of two to seven.
==Taxonomy==
It was first named in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as ''Lavatera arborea'',<ref name=apni>{{APNI2|id=164766|name=''Malva arborea''}}</ref><ref name=L>{{cite book|author=Linnaeus, C.|date=1753|title= Species Plantarum |volume=2|pages=690|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358711}}</ref> but was transferred to the genus ''[[Malva]]'' in 1836 by [[Philip Barker-Webb]] and [[Sabin Berthelot]].<ref name=apni/><ref name=webb>{{cite web|author=Webb, P.B. & Berthelot, S.|date=1836|title= Histoire Naturelle des Iles Canaries|volume= 3|issue=2,1|pages= 30|url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/9609/?offset=#page=34&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=}}</ref>

Although long considered a species of ''[[Lavatera]]'', genetic and morphological analysis by Martin Forbes Ray, reported in 1998, suggested it was better placed in the genus ''[[Malva]]'', in which it was named ''Malva dendromorpha'' M.F.Ray.<ref>Ray, Martin Forbes. (Autumn, 1998.) [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3392022 New Combinations in Malva (Malvaceae: Malveae).] ''Novon'' 8 (3): 288–295. {{doi|10.2307/3392022}}. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref><ref>Germplasm Resources Information Network: [http://www.ars-grin.gov/~sbmljw/cgi-bin/taxon.pl?412549 ''Malva dendromorpha''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924161059/http://www.ars-grin.gov/~sbmljw/cgi-bin/taxon.pl?412549 |date=2015-09-24 }} Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref> However the earlier name ''Malva arborea'' (L.) Webb & Berthel. was validly published and has priority over ''Malva dendromorpha''.

==Habitat==
''Malva arborea'' tolerates sea water to varying degrees, at up to 100% sea water in its natural habitat, excreting salt through glands on its leaves.<ref name="veitch2002">Veitch, C. R., and Michael Norman Clout (editors). (2002.) [https://portals.iucn.org/library/efiles/documents/ssc-op-028.pdf ''Turning the Tide: The Eradication of Invasive Species'': Proceedings of the International Conference on Eradication of Island Invasives.] The World Conservation Union (IUCN): Gland, Switzerland and Cambridge, UK, pp. 254–259. {{ISBN|2-8317-0682-3}}. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref><ref name="okusanya1985">Okusanya, O. T., and T. Fawole. (March 1985.) [https://www.jstor.org/stable/2259785 The Possible Role of Phosphate in the Salinity Tolerance of Lavatera Arborea.] The Journal of Ecology, Vol. 73, No. 1, pp. 317–322, {{doi|10.2307/2259785}}, Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref> This salt tolerance can be a competitive advantage over inland plant species in coastal areas. Its level of [[salinity]] tolerance is thought to be improved by soil with higher [[phosphate]] content, making [[guano]] enrichment particularly beneficial.<ref name="okusanya1985" /> It grows mainly on exposed coastal locations, often on small [[island]]s, only rarely any distance inland.<ref name=mp/><ref name=Botanica/><ref name=Vermeulen>Nico Vermeulen: ''The Complete Encyclopedia of Container Plants'' p. 158. Rebo International, Netherlands, 1998. {{ISBN|90-366-1584-4}}</ref><ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name=rhs>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan {{ISBN|0-333-47494-5}}.</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves of the species are used in herbal medicine to treat sprains, by steeping them in hot water and applying the [[poultice]] to the affected area.<ref>Rippey, Elizabeth and Barbara Rowland. (2004.) [https://books.google.com/books?id=12loNHZQr_0C&dq=Lavatera.arborea+sprains&pg=PA153 Coastal Plants: Perth and the South-west Region, 2nd Edition.] University of Western Australia Press, p. 153. {{ISBN|1-920694-05-6}}. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref> It is theorised that [[lighthouse]] keepers may have spread the plant to some British islands for use as a poultice and to treat burns, an occupational hazard.<ref>Royal Irish Academy  (1883.) [https://books.google.com/books?id=v1QFAAAAQAAJ&dq=Lavatera.arborea+lighthouse&pg=PA370 Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy, Second Series, Volume III: Science] Royal Irish Academy: Dublin, pp. 370, 375. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref><ref>[http://www.ceh.ac.uk/treemallow/what/index.html Tree Mallow: What is Tree Mallow?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070711202123/http://www.ceh.ac.uk/treemallow/what/index.html |date=2007-07-11 }} (Website). ''Invasion of Scottish seabird islands by tree mallow'', Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, UK Natural Environment Research Council. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref>
Thought to have been used as an alternative to toilet paper. The seeds are edible and are known in French as "petit pains", or "little breads".

Tree mallow was considered a nutritive animal food in Britain in the 19th century, and is still sometimes used as animal [[fodder]] in Europe.<ref name="veitch2002" /> For human consumption, some sources describe the leaves of tree mallow as edible, although not as palatable as common mallow, unless cut very thinly, because of the very velours-like hairy mouth-feel.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Knox|first1=Johanna|title=A forager's treasury|date=2013|isbn=9781877505164|pages=91, 92|publisher=Allen & Unwin |url=http://foragerstreasury.blogspot.co.nz/}}</ref>

''Malva arborea'' has long been cultivated in British gardens, as described in the 1835 self-published book ''British Phaenogamous Botany'', which used the then-common name ''Sea Tree-mallow'': "This species is frequently met with in gardens, where, if it is allowed to scatter its seeds, it will spring up for many successive years, and often attain a large size. The young plants will, as Sir J. E. Smith observes, now and then survive one or more mild Winters; but having once blossomed it perishes."<ref name=baxter>Baxter, William. (1835). [https://books.google.com/books?id=hBUAAAAAQAAJ&dq=tree.mallow+medicinal&pg=PT6 ''British Phaenogamous Botany, Or, Figures and Descriptions of the Genera of British Flowering Plants'' Vol. II.] (Self-published): Oxford, pp. 112-113. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref>

While sometimes detrimental to seabird habitat, management of tree mallow (both planting and thinning) has been successfully employed to shelter nesting sites of the threatened [[roseate tern]], which requires more coverage than [[common tern]]s to impede predation.<ref>Du Feu, Chris. (February 2005.) [http://www.bto.org/notices/nestbox.pdf Nestboxes: Extracts from British Trust for Ornithology Field Guide Number 23 with some additions and amendments.] British Trust for Ornithology, Norfolk, England, via bto.org. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref><ref>Newton, S. F. and O. Crowe. (April 2000.) [http://www.marine.ie/NR/rdonlyres/ACE02836-760C-4A74-817D-3771C5FE54E9/0/interreg2.pdf Roseate Terns – The Natural Connection: A conservation/research project linking Ireland and Wales.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071119131232/http://www.marine.ie/NR/rdonlyres/ACE02836-760C-4A74-817D-3771C5FE54E9/0/interreg2.pdf |date=2007-11-19 }} Maritime (Ireland / Wales) INTERREG Programme, p. 6. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref>

==Invasive spread==
Tree mallow seeds may be transported between separated coastal areas by the floating fruit, and seabirds are considered a likely means of spread. The seeds are encased in an impermeable outer case, and can remain viable for years, even after extended immersion in saltwater.<ref name="veitch2002" />

The tree mallow's recent increased range among Scottish islands has raised concerns that it is displacing native vegetation, and is reducing [[Atlantic puffin]] (''Fratercula arctica'') populations in affected areas. The plant forms dense stands along the island coasts that inhibit breeding, and causes the puffins to abandon their burrows.<ref>McKie, Robin. (2005-12-18) [https://www.theguardian.com/science/2005/dec/18/biodiversity.conservationandendangeredspecies Puffins being wiped out as shrub chokes nesting sites.] (News website.) ''Guardian Unlimited'', Guardian News and Media Limited. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref><ref>[http://www.ceh.ac.uk/treemallow/index.html Invasion of Scottish seabird islands by tree mallow.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070711201854/http://www.ceh.ac.uk/treemallow/index.html |date=2007-07-11 }} (Website.) Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, UK Natural Environment Research Council. Retrieved on 2007-09-28.</ref>

Its spread among Australian islands in recent decades is thought to be reducing biodiversity, soil retention, and seabird habitat. According to one study, "Crested and Caspian Terns that nest in the open are closed out by the canopy, and Little Penguins (''Eudyptula minor'') and Bridled Terns (''Sterna anaethetus'') are excluded by the lack of undergrowth".<ref name="veitch2002" />

In New Zealand it has established on several seabird-dominated islands where it is considered to be a serious ecological weed and for which there are active eradication programmes, such as on North Brother Island in Cook Strait.
